extracted.intended_audience: computer science researchers and graduate students writing papers/books/technical reports
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and preparing computer-science research papers, survey articles, technical reports, and book expositions, with advice on audience, structure, style, proofreading, and publication venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the market and know thyself / avoid slavish imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't slavishly imitate another's style; know the market, know thyself, and work out a compromise of your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one paper starts with 'write' and another with 'while', you don't have to copy either; be different but don't avoid imitation completely. Don't hesitate to follow the crowd when they are going in the right direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism vs imitation / explicit quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation becomes culpable if a reasonable person could not believe you didn't have the other work open; you can't copyright ideas, only ways of expressing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit in quotations if you feel more comfortable doing so. Beware of verbatim copying (even successive equations) — identical notation or typographical choices can be damning. Survey papers may contain verbatim quotes because the writer is not presenting the work as his own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate motives to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid two bad reasons for writing a paper: (1) to have a long publications list, and (2) to have a paper published in a specific conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reason to publish: 'You have done something that you are excited about.' Publishing for CV padding or to force a paper into particular proceedings can lead to sloppy work; appeal to personal integrity to police motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right venue (audience and place to publish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to publish as a Tech Report, letter, Journal article, conference paper, or leave in the drawer depending on readiness and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal articles should be polished and timeless; conference papers can be a little rougher and are appropriate for work 'not yet ready for the archives'; technical reports are for work not ready for the general world but still worth writing up. Remember readers exist in each case — a tech report may later become a journal article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely to learn writing (learn by reading great literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to write is more like learning to play the piano: you learn by reading — study great literature to learn how to write good mathematical literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport pays homage to Halmos and Knuth but recommends reading Fowles and Eliot as well; spend more time away from the instrument (keyboard) studying examples of excellent writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your idea before writing / fix ideas, not sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad writing comes from bad thinking; you must know what you want to present before you can present it well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't 'fix the sentence and not the idea.' Focus on structure and the underlying idea rather than on formatting or surface sentence tweaks during initial drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Use analogy, metaphor, and simile where you are sure the reader will get the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CS expositions generally use less analogy than some fields (e.g., physics), but analogy can be a useful catalyst if it clarifies rather than intrudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jokes and dated humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of jokes: how funny will a joke be ten years after inclusion in a journal paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes can date a paper; prefer enduring devices such as examples and clear exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples — one solid example is better than dry abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to have one solid example than to have a dry, abstract, academic paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple examples are never a mistake (especially for lectures). Examples keep you honest: a counterexample may reveal weaknesses in your theory and force revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't think about format; think about structure
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Don't think about format. Do think about structure.' — focus on the logical organization rather than formatting during composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defer formatting concerns (fonts, layout) until after the structure is right. Use macros for complex notation so formatting doesn't impede writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use macros for complex notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have details such as complex notation, do not write them out repeatedly — use a macro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This keeps drafts cleaner and lets you change notation globally later without retyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured/tabular proofs where helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabular 'statement–reason' forms (like high-school geometry proofs) can make structure clearer and help clarify paragraph proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both paragraph form and tabular form when useful; tabular structure enforces clarity and can help trim bloated prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sentence: be excited, nontechnical, direct, avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sentence should 'leap out at you', be nontechnical, and represent an author's best effort; avoid 'passive wimpiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a simple, direct opening that grabs the reader; sustain that energy so subsequent sentences do not disappoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain momentum throughout the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first sentence 'socks it to them,' you can't let them down with the second; maintain engaging writing by induction through the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each later sentence must continue to deliver value and clarity (Lamport: 'When you come to sentence number 2079, you've got to keep socking it to them').

rubrics_metrics.name: Start early and rewrite repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin writing early and be prepared to write, rewrite, rewrite, rewrite; most writers must labor over and over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat early drafts as sketches to be discarded or heavily revised; very few works are final on first draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never publish without external critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let anything you write be published without having had others critique it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the university environment or colleagues for feedback; be mindful of timing and the availability of willing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the topic while writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach a course on a topic at the time you are writing it up; teaching forces organisation and prevents inflicting ramblings on the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching helps discover holes in exposition and clarifies your internal model of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the reader / develop internal daemons
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask what the reader's primitives are and write with them in mind; run many 'daemons' in the background that catch errors and misunderstandings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how the reader will misunderstand you; develop automatic checks (like red flags for split infinitives) so you don't consciously run through a checklist while writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the medium (vocabulary, typography, figures, indices)
rubrics_metrics.description: You need a good vocabulary and understanding of issues beyond language: indexes, tables, graphs, typography and how to use them effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typography (e.g., typewriter font for logical formulae) to make important distinctions; be aware that future reading/writing will be more interactive and may require new stable practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the material — writing clarifies understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing provides internal feedback — organizing material for publication often leads to a new understanding of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in lectures and talks; the process of explaining and organizing helps form an 'internal model' and refines the exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify initial presentation, elaborate later
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the reader with something straightforward to start; you can 'lie' (simplify) initially and add correct details later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple examples to capture 80% of the truth with 20% of the difficulty; later expand with more precise or general formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recycling old text; rewrite for new context
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist reusing portions of old material unmodified; you are likely writing in a new context and should rewrite accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you are older and wiser, rewrite old material to fit the new emphasis and audience; it's worth the effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for excellence — continually improve
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep shooting for perfection even though you'll never reach it; demand the best in everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the mindset of relentless improvement — 'good' is not enough; always revise toward a better result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence length and variety targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for adult-writing averages under 20 words per sentence (ideal 15–18); ensure variation in sentence length for appropriate pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sampling the first 10 complete sentences on page three, aim for 9–10 different lengths; the distribution should resemble a bell curve centered 15–18 words. A few short 'punchy' sentences and some long ones are important; avoid having a 46-word sentence as your crucial point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence constructions (avoid repeated templates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the same sentence construction repeatedly (e.g., adverbial + subject + transitive verb + object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study sentence templates used in your writing; diversify construction so prose does not become monotonous. Beware of unusual syntactic usages and do not overuse them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tight parallels to communicate similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two adjacent sentences with exactly the same construction as an effective method to communicate similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique (tight parallels) is underused but powerful for emphasising sameness; learn to apply it deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic sentences are a high literary form — use sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic sentences (where grammatical and physical ends coincide) are a high literary form and generally not appropriate for mathematical or typical technical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic sentences may heighten control over sentence structure but are better suited to high literary contexts (e.g., church) than conference papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place emphasis at sentence front or back; middle is weak
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphatic positions in a sentence are the front and the back; the middle of a sentence is 'sort of a slum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast sentences to move important information to front or end to change emphasis; experiment to discover effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual-labor composition techniques (copying, typing, memorizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual work such as typing out passages, copying by hand, memorization and recitation help slow the brain and force careful reading and appreciation of structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These techniques train the 'manual' aspect of writing: practice copying other people's writing in different modes to tighten reading skills. They are analogous to drilling in other motor skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud, form critique partnerships, and use 'frozen sounds' detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your writing aloud and pair with other novice writers: listening reveals problems (frozen sounds) and helps detect defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partners should read and listen to each other's work; use small doses of feedback. Reading aloud can both embarrass weak prose and validate good writing; it helps reveal voice, stance, and tone issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion, verse, and précis exercises to build concision and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Scansion and verse-writing exercises are difficult but important; précis exercises force structural reworking to reduce word count without changing meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicing verse can heighten sensitivity to rhythm and scansion; in précis work you will need to change the structure of the prose to shorten it while preserving meaning — some details may be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to correct published work in later editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent editions consume time but allow reuse of earlier examples and can reinvigorate sales and correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second and later editions go faster if you reuse earlier examples; financial advantages exist because new editions restart buyers' interest; be prepared to correct mistakes found post-publication.
